en: Now, the ritual for the funeral rites (*antyeṣṭi*) of the body of a deceased Vajrācārya is described.
Having prostrated before the goddess named Locanā...

I shall describe the *mṛtasaṃjīvanī*, which is devoted to the welfare of others; the applications for reviving the dead, the assignments of the deceased to their destinies, and the directing of the dead toward happy rebirths.

In a well-isolated house of the deceased, the yogin—equipped with all ritual offerings, wearing a white-flowered turban (*uṣṇīṣa*), anointed with white perfumes, peaceful, and adorned with white garments and ornaments—should face the east while maintaining that visualization; or else, holding a vajra and vajra-bell, he should stand upon a high, soft seat. Having smeared a mandala in front with white sandalwood and other perfumes mixed with the water of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), he should decorate it with white flowers.
One should consecrate the water for the guest-offering (*argha*) and so forth with one's own mantras, ending in *svāhā* and accompanied by exhortations.
Having visualized one's own seed-syllable within the moon at the heart, one should protect the place and so forth.
In this regard, the mantra for protecting the yoga of the place and the self is as follows:
"Oṃ āḥ vighnāntakṛt hūṃ," or "Homage to Samanta... and so forth.

Having made this aspiration, the yogin should, according to the rule and according to the ritual procedure, emit the well-perfected wheel and the goad from the tip of the seed-syllable at the heart of Locanā.
O friend, this is the pure, red knowledge abiding in the world beyond;
it has the form of the merit of the Dharma, resembling a lamp that is unshaken by the wind.
One should bring that gnosis and cause it to enter the heart of the deceased through the crown of the head.
Thereupon, having arisen, one should see [the deceased] seated, endowed with gnosis.
Having cast the syllable *moharati* into his heart, one should perceive his body—rendered empty by a blazing garland of its rays—as consisting of nothing but representation (*vijñapti*).
Thereafter, reciting "moharati" and meditating upon that form of Locanā,
one should perform the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of her eyes and so forth, as well as her body and so forth, in every respect.

One should sprinkle her with nectar from the clouds of goddesses— emanated from the root mantra situated on the moon in the heart of the Wisdom Deity (*jñānadevatā*)— using jars consisting of a mass of light.
Then, one should sprinkle [the disciple] with clouds of eyes, which are emitted from one's own body, pervading the entire circle of the sky, and flashing forth in the form of masses of rays.

He should likewise consecrate him with his own vessel filled with water over which his mantra has been recited; he should then place a crown upon his head and bestow a vajra and bell in his two hands.

Thereafter, the mantra-practitioner, having visualized the tip of a blade of kusha grass as a sharp, single-pointed vajra, should insert it into the vajra-aperture and meditate upon it as resembling fire.

Thereafter, with the mind composed (*samāhitacetāḥ*), one should impel the throbbing gnosis deposited within that heart by means of blazing vajra-tips surrounded by winds. [The gnosis] is liquefied like mercury touched by the flames of fire;
released through the upward path, it enters either a pure Buddha-field or, otherwise, according to its knowledge, falls into the ocean of saṃsāra.

Therefore, one should effect its departure by way of the upper path: through the crown of the head, one goes to the Formless Realm (*ārūpya*); through the tuft of hair between the brows (*ūrṇākośa*), to what is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); through the two eyes, to the state of a human; through the two ears, to the destiny of a Siddha or a god; through the two nostrils, to the state of a Yakṣa or a Gandharva;
and one should emerge through the mouth.
Through the navel [one goes] to the state of the Kāmasaras; through the apāna [wind], to the realm of hungry ghosts (pretas);
through the path of urine, to animal birth; and through the path of excrement, to the state of hell.
Semen would surely go forth;
therefore, one should avoid those paths.

Then, for the sake of establishing him in the city of liberation, the Vajrācārya— having been provided with all the requisites of a preceptor (*ācārya*)— should perform a pacifying fire-offering (*śāntikahoma*) in the fire of primordial wisdom (*jñānāgni*), according to the complete ritual prescribed for the *śāntikahoma* or according to the procedure described for a single substance.
Furthermore, at that time, he should cause [the candidate] to recite Mahāyāna sūtras such as the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Thereafter, having gathered everything together, one should request the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) from the officiant (*yājaka*).

The officiant, in turn, should respectfully give the preceptor (*ācārya*) a sacrificial fee consisting of garments, ornaments, beds, seats, houses, fields, male and female slaves, laborers, and so forth, according to his means.
Then, having summoned those who performed the funeral rites, he should cause them to wear sacred threads (*yajñopavīta*) over which the three-syllable mantra has been recited.

Then, having visualized the world-protectors as the bearers of the corpse: the king of gods as the umbrella-bearer, Brahmā as the chowrie-wielder, Viṣṇu as the sword-bearer, Śaṅkara as the reciter of praises, Yama as the performer of the funeral rites (*ūrdhvadehika-kriyākāraka*), Varuṇa as the vessel-bearer, Agni as the bearer of the *śruva*-ladle and the various foods and edibles, and Nairṛti as the banner-bearer...
One should direct one’s resolve (*adhimucyet*) toward the wind that sustains the atmosphere (*vātādhara*), as well as toward all other gods, asuras, and so forth.
Then, having recited the hundred-syllable mantra one hundred and eight times and having dedicated one’s own merit toward perfect awakening (*samyaksaṃbodhi*), one should rise.

Having arisen, the Vajrācārya, whose intrinsic nature is that of the Vajradhara and who is the progenitor of all Buddhas, should proceed in front while reciting the mantra of Locanā or the mantras for the purification of all miserable rebirths as taught in the *Durgatipariśodhana-tantra*, or those mantras to be described below.

And along the way, he should visualize [the deceased] being led by the hosts of World-Protectors, being refined in the intermediate state (*uparataka*), and being incessantly worshipped by gods and others.

Accompanied by the sounds of various musical instruments, auspicious verses, and songs such as the *aśanīgīta*, followed by the resonance of bells, cymbals, flutes, and lutes, and provided with the fivefold offerings, banners, cloths, and leaves, one should slowly lead [the corpse] to the charnel ground (*pitṛvana*) amidst a great multitude of attendants.
There, having constructed a beautiful funeral pyre with dry milk-wood fuel and having placed the deceased upon it, one should sprinkle it there with water from a ritual jar (*kalaśa*).
Then, by means of the prescribed rite, one should kindle the fire.
There, at the heart of the corpse, one should offer three full oblations (*pūrṇāhuti*).
And for the purpose of satisfying the fire, one should cast in scented oil and so forth;
until it is reduced to ashes, the heir remains well-composed.
As before, one should cause them to recite the Mahāyāna sūtra of great success,
and have them sing the vajra-song following the *kāṃsī* and *ḍamaruka* instruments.
Then, certain people, being directed toward the path of liberation, do not proceed along a wrong path because their wholesome [roots] are more abundant and powerful.

Therefore, in order to prevent that person from proceeding upon an evil path, one should perform the rites for purifying the miserable destinies (*durgatipariśodhana*) and so forth, beginning from that day for eight days, according to the procedure taught in the *Durgatipariśodhana-tantra*.
During that time, as long as the bones have not been brought, one should perform the rite upon the cloth [bearing the image], preceded by the recitation of the name.
Once those bones and the cloth have been brought, however, one should perform it until the eighth day.
And there, on the southern side, having prepared a square altar (*vedi*) measuring one cubit, smeared with fresh cow dung, one should sprinkle it with products of the cow (*gavya*).

Having anointed that area and fashioned a mandala adorned with flowers from the *Arjuna* and *Malaya* trees, one should place upon it a ritual jar (*kalaśa*) endowed with the proper characteristics, filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), medicinal herbs, sprouts, jewels, fragrant substances, and rice.

One should consecrate a large [image] that is joined with an umbrella and banner, has a blue cloth around its neck, is provided with the five offerings, fumigated, joined with water from sacred fords (*tīrtha*), placed upon a seat made of *darbha* grass, and marked with the insignia of the Lord of the Family (*kulapati*).
Then, the mantra-practitioner should [consecrate] it one hundred and eight times with the root seed-syllable (*mūlabīja*) joined with the three syllables, or with the washing mantra.

Then, having drawn an eight-spoked wheel with its hub and rim in white flour before him, blazing with light and strewn with white flowers, he should place a perforated shallow bowl (*śarāva*) upon an empty jar in the center of that [wheel].
Thereafter, he should place those bones in that bowl without leaving any remainder.
Having performed the three prescribed meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), he should perform the *Pratyaṅgirā* rite for him.
Reciting the mantras in sequence with *siddhārtha* seeds and flowers while responding to each, one should strike that bone; this is called the "Armor" (*prāvaraṇa*) rite for it.
Now, the mantra words are:
*oṃ sarvapāpadahanavajra hūṃ phaṭ*.
Oṃ, vajra that purifies all sins, hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ, reduce all karmic obscurations to ashes, hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ bhrūṃ, destroy the obscurations, jaṃ hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ hūṃ, purify all obscurations, hūṃ phaṭ! Oṃ, all karmic obscurations, hūṃ phaṭ!
Oṃ jvala 2 dhaka 2 hana 2 āvaraṇāni hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ bhrūṃ sara 2 prasara 2 āvaraṇāni hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ hūṃ hara 2 sarvāvaraṇāni hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ hūṃ, shatter all obscurations! Hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ bhṛta 2, all obscurations! Hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ trāṭa 2 sarvāvaraṇāni hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ chinda 2 sarvāvaraṇāni hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ daha 2 sarvanarakagatihetūn hūṃ phaṭ.
Oṃ paca 2 all causes for the state of hungry ghosts hūṃ phaṭ. Oṃ matha 2 all causes for the state of animals hūṃ phaṭ.
This is the mantra for striking with bones and so forth.
Then, one should wash those bones and so forth with the water from the consecrated flask while reciting the mantra.
The mantra is:

Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the King who Purifies All Evil Destinies, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. It is thus: Oṃ, purifier, purifier; thorough purifier, thorough purifier; O purifier of all sins, pure one, thoroughly pure one! Purify all karmic obscurations, svāhā! This is the mantra for washing the bones and so forth. Then, having scattered flowers while reciting the mantra, one should show the path.
The mantra is: Oṃ ratne ratne ratnasaṃbhave ratnakiraṇe ratnamālāviśuddhe śodhaya śodhaya sarvapāpaṃ hūṃ trāṭ.
This is the mantra for the vision of the destinies.
Then, having sprinkled water with flowers, one should purify the path.
The mantra is: *oṃ padme padme padmodbhave sukhāvatyāṃ gacchantu svāhā*.
This is the mantra for purifying the path. In each of those mantra phrases, one should insert the word "water. With this mantra for purifying the path, one should cause a rain of flowers to fall.
Being composed in mind, he should have auspicious verses (*maṅgalagāthā*) sung from the *geya* section;
likewise, he should perform this at the three junctions of the day or at one junction every day.
Having thus performed the worship, he should withdraw all [the deities] according to the prescribed ritual procedure.
In this regard, there is this verse of auspiciousness:
That which is the auspiciousness of the Buddha— who delights in the welfare of all sentient beings, who is free from faults, and whose awakening is pure—
May that auspiciousness belong to you during the supreme consecration— you who delight in the engagement of the limbs of wisdom and whose nature is bliss.

Whatever blessing belongs to the Dharma— worshipped by gods, humans, and asuras, spoken by the Unsurpassed One, renowned throughout the three worlds, and characterized by selflessness— by that [blessing]...
May that auspiciousness be yours for supreme advancement.
May there be auspiciousness for that assembly of noble sons of the Conqueror who uphold the powerful Dharma, who always abide on the true stages, who are virtuous,
and who have risen up, being skillful in benefiting sentient beings.
May that auspiciousness be yours at the supreme consecration.
Thus, these auspicious verses (*maṅgalagāthā*) should be sung or caused to be sung at the time of washing the bones.
Therein is the mantra for dismissal:
*oṃ kṛto vaḥ sarvasattvārthaṃ siddhiṃ dattvā yathānugā gacchadhvaṃ buddhaviṣayaṃ punar āgamanāya muḥ*.
Thus.

Then, having performed the *gaṇacakra* at night, one should withdraw everything. However, if there is wealth available, one should explain the Maṇḍala for Purifying the Evil Destinies according to the ritual rules and perform it according to the prescribed method.
Furthermore, having prostrated at the feet of the Vajrācārya, one should request a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). He, too, should give it according to his means.
And having washed a garment, one should offer it to the Ācārya in this manner.
And it is said:
"Whatever is given by one's kinsmen to a teacher on account of the deceased, that should be understood as given to him; it is the provisions for the journey of one who has gone to heaven."
Whatever may be given by those seeking Śiva within seven days,
by that gift he will certainly be honored in Sukhāvatī.

Thus, when all the funeral rites have been performed according to the prescribed rule, one certainly attains Sukhāvatī, having abandoned all sins. Thereafter, having purified those bones by grinding them into an extremely fine powder with a stone, one should cast them into a very broad river after worshipping and honoring them; or else, having ascended the highest peak of a great mountain, one should scatter that powder there, carried away by the force of the surrounding wind.

If, due to the power of extremely cruel karma, one does not go to Sukhāvatī, the bestower of bliss, then by means of the ritual procedure for the final offering (*iṣṭi*) to the Nirvṛta-Vajrācārya, that person will certainly go to the abode of the Thirty-three gods, having abandoned the miserable states of existence.
Thus, this collection of the master’s rites, which is like nectar to me— having been gathered with effort from various scriptures and traditions like flowers from the Gaṅgā—

and which is the cause for the accumulation of merit on the great stages of a Son of the Victor (*jinatanaya*), may all beings through it attain the light of the three worlds, the vast palace of supreme joy belonging to the Victors.
Thus ends the *Ācāryakriyāsamuccaya*.
This work is the composition of the learned Avadhūta Śrīdarpaṇa, the master of the great maṇḍala who has explained [this text].
